parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem: State the property of an object that experiences a force when the object is placed in:
hints: Hint 1: Think about what it is about any object that lets gravity pull on it, even when the object has no charge and is not magnetic.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What feels a gravitational pull**
Any object with mass feels a force $F = mg$ in a gravitational field of strength $g$. Mass is the property that couples to gravity, so that is the answer here.

walkthrough:

An object feels a force $F = Eq$ in an electric field of strength $E$ only if it carries net electric charge $q$. Charge is the property that couples to the electric field.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A potential difference of $1.2 \times 10^3\text{ V}$ is applied between a pair of horizontal metal plates in a vacuum, as shown in Fig. 3.1.

{{figure:figure_3_1}}

Fig. 3.1 (not to scale)

The separation of the plates is $3.6\text{ cm}$. The electric field between the plates is uniform.

A particle of mass $5.9 \times 10^{-6}\text{ kg}$ and charge $-4.2 \times 10^{-9}\text{ C}$ enters the field at point $X$ with a horizontal velocity of $0.75\text{ m s}^{-1}$ along a line midway between the two plates. The particle is deflected by the field and hits the top plate at point $Y$.
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the electric force acting on the particle in the field.
hints: Hint 1: You are given the voltage across the plates and their separation, and told the field is uniform. Think about how field strength links those two quantities.
Hint 2: Use $$E = \frac{V}{d}$$ to get $E$, then use $$F = Eq$$ to get the force on charge $q$. Remember to convert $d = 3.6\text{ cm}$ to metres.
Hint 3: Take magnitudes only for the size of the force. Combine the two steps as $$F = \frac{Vq}{d}$$ and check powers of ten carefully.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Field strength between the plates**
Between parallel plates the field is uniform, so the strength depends only on voltage $V$ and plate separation $d$. Convert $d$ first: $$d = 3.6\text{ cm} = 3.6 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$$ Then: $$E = \frac{V}{d} = \frac{1.2 \times 10^{3}}{3.6 \times 10^{-2}} \approx 3.33 \times 10^{4}\text{ V m}^{-1}$$ directed from positive top plate to negative bottom plate.

Step 2: **Force on the charge**
A charge of magnitude $|q| = 4.2 \times 10^{-9}\text{ C}$ feels: $$F = |q|E = \frac{V|q|}{d}$$ So: $$F = \frac{(1.2 \times 10^{3})(4.2 \times 10^{-9})}{3.6 \times 10^{-2}} = 1.4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ N}$$ The negative sign tells you the direction is upward toward the positive plate, but magnitude is $1.4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ N}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: By considering the resultant vertical force acting on the particle, show that the acceleration of the particle in the electric and gravitational fields is $14\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
hints: Hint 1: In the vertical direction two forces act in opposite senses: the upward electric force and the downward weight. Sketch both arrows first.
Hint 2: Calculate the weight from the given mass using $W = mg$ with $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$ and compare its size with $1.4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ N}$.
Hint 3: Find the resultant upward force by subtracting the smaller downward force from the larger upward force.
Hint 4: Use Newton's second law in the form $a = F_{net}/m$ with the same mass to show $a$ is about $14\text{ m s}^{-2}$ upwards.
parts.proper_answer: $W = 5.8 \times 10^{-5}\text{ N}$ downwards, $F_{net} \approx 8.2 \times 10^{-5}\text{ N}$ upwards, $a = F_{net}/m \approx 14\text{ m s}^{-2}$ upwards.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Weight acting downwards**
Mass always brings weight: $$W = mg$$ $$W = (5.9 \times 10^{-6})(9.81) \approx 5.79 \times 10^{-5}\text{ N}$$ This acts vertically down.

Step 2: **Resultant vertical force**
The electric force $F_E = 1.4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ N}$ acts up on the negative particle toward the positive top plate. Net upward force is: $$F_{net} = F_E - W$$ $$F_{net} = 1.4 \times 10^{-4} - 5.79 \times 10^{-5} \approx 8.2 \times 10^{-5}\text{ N}$$ Upwards, because the electric force is larger.

Step 3: **Acceleration from Newton's second law**
$$a = \frac{F_{net}}{m} = \frac{8.2 \times 10^{-5}}{5.9 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 13.9\text{ m s}^{-2}$$ This rounds to $14\text{ m s}^{-2}$ upwards, as required. Notice weight cannot be ignored here because the particle is relatively heavy.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Treat horizontal and vertical motions separately. Vertically the particle starts from rest and accelerates up at $14\text{ m s}^{-2}$ through $1.8\text{ cm}$ to reach the top plate.
Hint 2: Use $$s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^{2}$$ vertically with $u = 0$ and $s = 1.8 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$ to solve for the flight time $t$.
Hint 3: Horizontally there is no force, so velocity stays at $0.75\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Use distance = speed x time to get $p$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Time from vertical motion**
Vertical initial velocity is zero, vertical displacement to the top plate is: $$s = 1.8\text{ cm} = 1.8 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$$ With $u = 0$ and $a = 14\text{ m s}^{-2}$: $$s = \frac{1}{2}at^{2}$$ $$t = \sqrt{\frac{2s}{a}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.8 \times 10^{-2}}{14}} \approx 5.07 \times 10^{-2}\text{ s} \approx 0.051\text{ s}$$

Step 2: **Horizontal distance p**
There is no horizontal force in the vacuum, so horizontal velocity $v_x = 0.75\text{ m s}^{-1}$ is constant. In time $t$: $$p = v_x t = 0.75 \times 0.051 \approx 0.038\text{ m}$$ That is about $3.8\text{ cm}$ from the entry edge.
